speechtext:
Because of this experience, some of us began early in this session trying to pin the government down, to secure a firm undertaking that the government would go through with the implementation of the Canada pension plan. The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows what she said when I asked her the first few times about the plan. She told me to contain myself in patience, that I would soon see the bill. I kept on asking her. I put questions to her on this subject on May 20 and May 22, and each time I was told the legislation would come soon. Then, on June 8 the hon. lady went to Hamilton and made a speech before a Liberal organization down there giving details of the Canada pension plan which was to be introduced in the House of Commons. A couple of days later I asked her if she would be good enough to tell the house what she had told the Liberals in Hamilton. She assured me that the details of the plan would soon be placed before us. On June 19, incidentally, the 59th day this government was in office-everyone knows how those first 60 days went by-the minister did succeed in giving notice of the resolution preceding the bill to set up the Canada pension plan. It appeared on our notice paper on June 20, which was the 60th day the present government was in office. And the government was very proud that it had got that far in the first 60 days. But all of this is to be seen in the light of the election promise that Liberal government would be prepared to act promptly in this matter.
On June 21, the resolution was transferred from government notices of motion to government orders and it looked as though we were making progress. A few days later the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) sent his famous letter to the premiers of the provinces about questions of social security beyond old age security and beyond the Canada pension plan, which seemed to me to suggest that a way was being opened up for delay. So I asked the Prime Minister on June 26 whether the result of his letter might be to cause delay in the implementation of the Canada pension plan. The right hon. gentleman assured me that such would not be the case. That is the story over a considerable period of time. There was

the promise of action, confirmation of that promise, assurances that if we would just wait we would see the bill and get going. Finally, on July 18, the motion respecting the resolution preceding the bill to bring in the plan was moved by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. As hon. members all know, we had that one day's debate, and that is all the opportunity we have had for discussion of the matter in this house.
I would remind hon. members opposite that during the debate of July 18 the hon. lady said some interesting and significant things. She said the plan had been worked out in considerable detail, and I agree with her. She said that, provided the house could move with reasonable expedition in passing this legislation, it would be possible for contributions to the new plan to commence in October, 1964, and for certain of the benefits under the plan to begin in January, 1966. There were two main benefits which were to start in January, 1966. The first was to be payments under the pension plan itself of say, $10 a month, to people who had contributed for a couple of years and who had reached the age of 70. The other benefit would be the right of people to take a pension at an earlier age, such as 65 or any age between 65 and 70.
The point I wish to make is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare made it clear that, in order to get the plan going so that contributions could be made in October of 1964 and so that people could begin deriving benefits by January, 1966, the legislation had to be put through parliament as expeditiously as possible. Yet here we are at the end of October, having waited since July 18, and this house has not been given an opportunity to proceed further with that legislation.
All of us know what has happened in the meantime-the furore which has been raised about the plan, notably by the insurance companies and other private interests who think that pension plans of this sort should not be handled by the government. We know there have also been complaints by some of the provinces which resulted in this question being discussed at the federal-provincial conference held while the house was in summer recess. I recognize that, as a result of what took place at that conference, certain decisions were made and certain changes were made. It was decided at that time, I think partly because of what happened at the conference but partly because of protests which came from opposition parties and from people throughout the length and breadth of the country, to separate the $10 increase in old age security benefits from the Canada pension plan and to put it into effect forthwith. That was a good decision. That increase
Pension Legislation Delayed was brought in on September 30, or at least it was first moved on that date, and now it is part of the law of the land. But one of the byproducts of this change has been that nothing further has been done to go ahead with the Canada pension plan itself.
The minister may say there was an undertaking to consult with the provinces and that there is another federal-provincial conference coming up in the month of November to discuss this plan and other related matters. But surely we have the right to know the intention of the federal government with respect to this legislation, which is still on our order paper and concerning which nothing has been done since July 18. Attempts which have been made since we resumed on September 30 to extract from the Minister of National Health and Welfare or from the Prime Minister any kind of assurance that the measure will be proceeded with at this session have been utterly unsuccessful. This is so, despite the fact that the hon. lady herself pleaded, on July 18, for expedition so that the benefits of the plan could reach our people at the earliest possible date. On September 30, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare introduced a resolution providing for the $10 increase in old age security payments she said this, as reported in Hansard at page 3038:
This present measure is a solid step in the right direction but the government sincerely hopes that the Canada pension plan will be introduced before too long to provide adequately for the retirement of our older people.
During the election campaign there was no doubt about it. It would be done. According to the speech from the throne, it would be done. According to the speech made by the Prime Minister in the debate on the address, it would be done. Throughout May and June the minister told us to possess our souls in patience, because it would be done. But on September 30 the hon. lady merely hopes it will be introduced before too long.
By October 15 I was finding it difficult to possess my soul in patience much longer. So I asked the Prime Minister whether he could give us an assurance that the plan would be proceeded with during the present session. In reply, as is reported on page 3579 of Hansard for October 15, the right hon. gentleman said:
We intend to proceed with legislation In this matter as soon as possible.
The exchange continued:

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext: Would it be possible for the Prime Minister to say whether that "as soon as possible" means this session?

subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It depends among other things on the hon. gentleman and all hon. members of the house and how long we take over the legislation we are now considering.

Pension Legislation Delayed
This refers to legislation which had been promised, legislation which was considered so important that it was the keystone in the arch of the Liberal victory in April; it was something many people had counted on; it was legislation which they had been led to expect would be enacted promptly. Yet now it is given such low priority that time spent by hon. members in discussing almost any other matter is allowed to stand in the way of its implementation.
On October 18, as reported at page 3735 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister, because there had been a statement on this subject by Premier Robarts, whether we could have an assurance that the plan would be proceeded with at this session of parliament. His answer was:
I have already indicated that the Canada pension plan will be proceeded with as soon as possible.
I then asked as a supplementary question:
Is the Prime Minister aware of the fact that that answer has been interpreted as meaning the plan is to be put off until a later session? Can he not give a definite answer with respect to this session?
To this, the Prime Minister replied that he was not responsible for other people's interpretations. When my hon. friend from Bur-naby-Coquitlam made an observation to the effect that this interpretation was apparently being made by none other than the premier of Ontario, the Prime Minister replied:
Any interpretation of that kind that the plan will not be proceeded with at this session would certainly be premature.
He did not deny the interpretation. He just said it was too soon to put that kind of interpretation upon it. A few days later I asked the Prime Minister if he would give the house a line-up of the business to be dealt with during the balance of the session, and he indicated he would. It is no secret that one of the things I hoped he would include in that list was the Canada pension plan legislation. I got no satisfaction in that respect. On the orders of the day this afternoon, I asked the question whether in view of the statement which the Minister of National Health and Welfare made to the national Liberal women's federation yesterday, that the plan would be proceeded with either this session or at the next, the Prime Minister could tell us which it is to be-this session or next. He gave the same answer- "as soon as possible".
The other day in another exchange the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that the government is as interested as ever in the Canada pension plan and is discussing the matter with the provinces. Surely, Mr. Speaker, my grievance is quite clear that there is a world of difference between the assurance in the election campaign that it would be


proceeded with, between the categorical statement in the speech from the throne that it was coming, between the Prime Minister's assurance in his speech that these things would be proceeded with at this session, between the earlier statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare that her career was tied to this pension plan and if the pension plan went down she would go down too, between all of these assurances and the statements we are now getting that it will be as soon as possible, maybe this session, maybe next, and that the government is still interested in the Canada pension plan.
I think that statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare is really the pay-off. This is the government's baby. This is the keystone in the arch of the Liberal success at the last election. This was the one precise proposal. Most of the rest of the things that the Liberals talked about in the campaign, apart from the position they were going to take on nuclear arms, were in vague generalities. Here was something that was precise. But now, instead of its being something about which we can get a firm answer that the government is going ahead, we are told by the responsible minister, the minister who was prepared to tie her career to this, only that the government is still interested in the Canada pension plan. We contend that this house deserves more than that from the government. We contend that the people of Canada deserve more than that from the government. We contend that we have the right to the assurance that this plan is going to be proceeded with at this session of parliament.
As I have already said, the Minister of National Health and Welfare herself gave a timetable when she spoke on the 18th of July. Surely this makes it quite clear that if the plan is not proceeded with at this session, if it is put off until 1964, the whole timetable will have to be pushed along. That will mean that contributions will not start in the fall of 1964 but will start in 1965 or 1966 or 1967. Every year that the beginning of the contributions is put off puts off the first year in which benefits will be enjoyed by people who are reaching the age of 70. If the plan were carried forward as promised it would mean that people who are now 68 years of age could count on an addition to their old age security out of the Canada pension plan when they reach 70 and, of course, people 67, 66 and down could all count on such a supplement. But if the plan is put off it means that the 68-year olds can kiss that idea goodbye. It means it is gone for the 69-year-olds. It means we will have again another round of the whole need for raising the flat rate benefit of old age security itself.

I should like to stress this angle, that the whole question of getting our old age security on a good, firm, sound basis ought to be by means of combining a contributory plan with the flat rate benefit, and unless we do it at a time like this we are going to have to change the relationship, change the calculations, increase the old age security benefit again and go through the whole round with all the difficulties we have had.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that not only was this one of the major promises in the Liberal platform at the last election, but that it is the most important domestic issue that has been placed before parliament. As I say, it was put on the order paper back on the 20th or 21st of June and was first debated on the 18th of July. But now it stands waiting while the government tries to make up its mind whether it is just interested in the plan or whether it is really going to go ahead with it.
A good deal gets said in the course of all this about the position of the province of Quebec and the position of the province of Ontario. The federal government talks more about Ontario than it talks about Quebec, although Mr. Lesage is making it just as difficult to bring this plan into being as is Mr. Robarts. But I should like to make the point that Mr. Robarts' statements have been pretty clear. There was a real fight over this matter in the recent Ontario election and an attempt was made to cast Mr. Robarts in the role of being an opponent of the Canada pension plan. Maybe in some respects he was. Maybe he preferred his plan. But since the election he has given a clear indication that if the Canada pension plan is going to be brought in his government will delay the implementation of the portable pension plan proposed for Ontario. But he has said that if the Canada pension plan is not put through at this session, if it is shelved, then Ontario will have no option but to bring in its plan and to provide for it to become effective perhaps in 1965.
It seems to me that is not a threat on the part of Mr. Robarts. I am the last person in the house who feels any need to defend Mr. Robarts, but I suggest we need to look at this thing fairly. He has not posed any threat. As a matter of fact, he has left the door open for the federal government to bring in its plan at this session. He is trying to hurry the federal government along. I understand that the Ontario government has named its members to a committee to discuss the technical aspects of the whole business with the federal government, and it seems to me that so far as public representatives are concerned, so far as the public view is concerned, the time is ripe for the plan to be proceeded with at this session of parliament.
Pension Legislation Delayed
I urge, Mr. Speaker, that we do not continue to be given these "as soon as possible" answers, that we do not continue to be told that the government is merely interested and, above all, I suggest that the government must not use the excuse that it cannot get on with this business because the house does not deal with other matters as expeditiously as it would like. As I pointed out when I put a question to the Prime Minister the other day, there are 20 or 25 items of business on the order paper. When house business is announced there are never more than four or five referred to. There are another 15 or 20 that are never suggested. We may get some light on the government's intentions on Monday, but so far we have no list of priorities. We feel this subject should be given top priority and that there should be no further delay in assuring the house that it will be proceeded with at this session.
I am prepared to hear the government say that the motion cannot be proceeded with until after the federal-provincial talks have been held in the month of November, but there is no question but that this session of parliament is going to last quite a bit longer than that. I think we are all assuming we will be here pretty well up to Christmas eve, if not longer, and I think we should have the positive assurance of the government that as soon as the November talks are over this plan will be proceeded with.
Obviously some changes are going to have to be made. The resolution that is still on the order paper and which was debated on the 18th of July does not take into consideration the fact that a $10 increase has now been made in old age security payments. It does not take into consideration the opting out that Premier Lesage has expressed on behalf of Quebec. These facts have got to be met. Let us have them met. Let us have a new resolution introduced. Let us have a new actuarial report similar to that excellent one prepared by the government actuary, so that we will have that picture up to date.
In my view the Minister of National Health and Welfare has done a good job in trying to answer attacks on the plan by the insurance companies. The speech that was made in her name in Toronto on Monday, September 30, by her parliamentary secretary, was an effective answer to the insurance companies' attacks on the plan. But in the meantime we read in the column in Maclean's magazine written by no less a friend of the Liberal party than Peter Newman that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has only five other members of the cabinet who still support her on this plan, and at the same time the Prime Minister himself says only "as soon as possible".

Pension Legislation Delayed
This, Mr. Speaker, is not good enough. This is an important item in the Liberal government program, but it is more than that. It is something that now belongs to the House of Commons. It is something that now belongs to the Canadian people. The responsibility for any further delay rests upon the government and I call upon the government for a clear statement that the plan will be proceeded with at this session of parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has raised as a grievance this evening the Canada pension plan and the fact that it has not proceeded through all stages in the house. He has asked as well for a clear statement that the government will proceed with the plan during this session which, as my hon. friend knows, perhaps has only another month or two to run. I should like to draw to my hon. friend's attention the agenda already before the house involving business which must be done, including even supply motions and all the estimates which must be brought forward and discussed.
My hon. friend will realize how little time is left for legislation between now and the end of this session. I ask him to bear that in mind as a framework in listening to the remarks which I should like to make this evening regarding the present status of the Canada pension plan.
There is no suggestion in the mind of the government that the plan is to be shelved. I know my hon. friend has spoken as he has and has raised this matter and sought an assurance from the government because of his interest in this social legislation. I know he does not raise it in an attempt to harm the possibility of such legislation being enacted for the benefit of the Canadian people. My hon. friend knows, I think, Mr. Speaker, that I am not, by nature, a patient individual. Indeed, some misguided individuals in this country have called me precipitate on occasion. Surely then, as the minister responsible for this legislation my hon. friend must realize that my inclination would be rather to press on with the matter. This being the case he will, and perhaps other members will, understand how if I am prepared to be patient, I have the temerity to ask him and other hon. members also to be patient.
In July of this year a resolution which was on the order paper was opened for debate, and a one day debate only was had upon it. This debate occasioned the rather unusual step, namely, the introduction of a white paper on the plan in order that information might be had abroad in the country as well

as in the house as quickly as possible concerning the framework of the Canada pension plan. My hon. friend knows the steps of legislation in this house much better than I, and he knows that normally we would have proceeded through the stages of the introduction of a bill in order for this amount of detail to be given. Since it was felt by the government that the details should be available as fully and as quickly as possible, a white paper was prepared and introduced on the first day of the resolution stage. This white paper set out broadly, and in some particularity, the intention of the government in respect of this legislation.
This was a matter which had priority; this was a matter included in the speech from the throne. But, Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend knows, there is a new spirit of co-operative federalism abroad in this country, one which requires and demands further consultation with the provinces than perhaps ever before occurred. I think my hon. friend will agree with most hon. members on both sides of the chamber that such consultation is good. The federal government must bear in mind that its responsibility is to enact federal legislation. But surely, sir, it is clear that when such legislation can be of the type which could collide with provincial legislation in some field it is necessary, so far as possible, to dovetail actions on the two levels.
Until this house rose for its adjournment, no new action had been taken in the pension field in the provinces. When this government came into authority, there had been a recent enactment by the province of Ontario. My hon. friend has made a study of pensions, I know, throughout much of his public career. He is aware of the type of legislation which was enacted, but is not yet in force, in Ontario. This particular type of legislation applies to only about one half of the labour force of that province. It incorporates, so far as it is possible in a province, that principle to which I think members on all sides of the house adhere, the portability of benefits from one job to another. But it is necessarily confined only to the province of Ontario.
It has still another problem which does not attract support to it from many quarters, that is it is not a state plan as such, not introduced, funded or supported in any way by a provincial government, but is a regulatory system only. It requires any employer of 15 or more people to bring into force a contributory pension plan calling for contributions, in most cases, from both employee and employer but without stating the amount of those contributions and setting minimal standards. The minimal standards would call for in some 40 years the payment of about

$80 a month to the individual contributor. There is nothing, of course, in the legislation to prohibit any employer-employee arrangement to provide for a greater pension. But because it is compulsory on the group with which it deals, care must be taken not to require too heavy a burden, particularly with the impact all at one time, upon the Ontario employer and employee.
Now, Mr. Speaker, at least the principle of a plan which is available to every person in the labouring force of Canada, to all 6.5 million people, is the kind of principle to which this house should be addressing itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
The figures to which I have had recourse are from a 1960 publication by the dominion bureau of statistics. This indicates that about 1.7 million people in our labour force have some kind of pension plan. This does not mean that they have a full pension plan with a decent standard of repayment, but simply means that they have some kind of a plan. 1 do not believe that 1.7 million people out of a labour force of 6.5 million is anything near sufficient opportunity for our Canadian labour force.
Within the province of Ontario, were the Ontario legislation to be proceeded with-and I do not suggest it is bad legislation-I would suggest that type of legislation does not go far enough. By virtue of the fact it is not compulsory for all the labour force, it does not occupy the field in so far as legislation for old age purposes is concerned. Therefore, there has been an invitation to Ontario to set aside to some degree its own legislation-this after all is a decision of the Ontario legislature and not even of the federal members from Ontario-in order that a truly universal Canadian pension plan might be brought into being.
My hon. friend has referred to some recent comments by the premier of Ontario. He knows that as a result of the conference which was set up in September of this year between the officials and ministers of each province and the federal government there arose, after two days of discussion, a decision to set up a technical committee to attempt to find a solution to the problems existing as between the Ontario and federal plans. I reported, I believe the other day, and can now tell my hon. friend, that the first meeting of this technical committee will be held this week. It is not a meeting of ministers or prime ministers but of technical people only. This will, in effect, be the third time upon which there has been some kind of dialogue between Ontario and federal authorities in the field of pensions.

The first, brief though it was, was at the conference held shortly after the introduction of the resolution on the Canada pension plan, in which the premiers attended with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and had some opportunity to deal with this situation. Hon. members will recall that the matter of the municipal loan legislation was also before that meeting, and because there was such a shortage of time it was agreed that there should be a further meeting at the department level. This was held early in September. Following it, as I say, there was a decision to set up the technical committee which is now meeting.
I think it is no secret to any member of this house that in the interval there has been a provincial election in the province of Ontario, and that while an election is in progress there is a hiatus in the provincial or federal field during which no decision can be made. Accordingly, we are encouraged that the technical committee which was set up will be meeting this week and we will have a further opportunity to discuss this matter in depth with all the provinces at the meeting, which is being held to discuss all facets of dominion-provincial relations, and particularly the economic facet. This meeting is to be held here on November 25. Presupposing there was complete unanimity between the provinces and the federal government, this meeting would probably take about a week.
My hon. friend will see, then, that there would be some three weeks left in the life of this particular session. I believe my hon. friend has been watching with some care the developments in relation to the Canada pension scheme and has seen, in fact he referred to it, considerable pressure built up against it in a lobby outside of this House of Commons. While all parties have been committed to the principle of a Canada-wide contributory pension scheme, we do not know and cannot know until a vote is called in the house, how each and every member of the house is committed to either this or some other comparable scheme. It is no secret that members have been receiving a considerable amount of correspondence, and in some cases visitations here and in their constituencies from individuals whose purpose is to see that the plan is not enacted.
Some of the remarks which have been made outside this house have been unhappily most intemperate. I do not attempt now to say that some of the intemperance is not on my own part, but I feel very devoutly about this type of legislation and the necessity for its immediate introduction for the welfare of our people. If I need to make an apology

Pension Legislation Delayed to the people of this country, it is only because I am so anxious they will have this opportunity that I have been perhaps somewhat intemperate in my remarks. But there are others who have far less excuse, others who from their position in years alone might be expected to deal with the matter in a different way.
We have had a type of document sent around the country which says, "let us create a storm"; language which has been careless in the extreme, and which on occasion has gone out of its way to indicate one point of view only, and to leave unsaid all those things which might be said on behalf of this type of scheme.
A government cannot at this stage use public funds or hire any individual to start producing glossy literature. A government has only its spokesmen and its members; but hon. members of the house have not seen the Canada pension plan, and indeed should not until we reach that stage of the legislative process where it is produced. That being the case everyone, and to some extent even the minister concerned, must feel in a vacuum, because until questions are resolved between the provinces and the federal government it is unfair to ask me to be dogmatic about certain points with respect to the plan.
I know members of parliament in all parties are anxious to go out on the hustings and talk to people in their constituencies about the benefits to be obtained, benefits which can only be obtained from a state run, universal, contributory pension scheme, but it is necessary for them to wait until that stage in the legislative process where the bill will be before them.
In the meantime public opinion is being engendered against such a scheme, and we have seen representatives of at least one industry producing material, sending it across the country, and attempting to influence people in a quasi-govemmental position in our communities. Many of the individuals who produce this material do so in good faith. They simply disagree violently with this in principle, and as free citizens in a free country they have a right to say so. It may be of some concern to some individuals as to exactly whose money they are using to promote their ideas, but that is not for them to answer in the House of Commons. They have to answer for that somewhere else.
There has been fear in some parts of the country that there may be an intolerable burden introduced upon the shoulders of the manufacturers, and a fear as well that the government has acted precipitously and without understanding the problems involved, and without the requisite amount of work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, someone says that is right. I can only assume the hon. member did not take time to read the very lengthy document which was circulated. Surely no member of the house in any party can object to the way the government has treated all hon. members in this regard. Not only was the white paper produced in both our official languages and sent to every member but, during our adjournment, the actuarial report, prepared after months of work by first class people in our public service, was sent to every member of parliament for perusal and study.
My hon. friend who speaks for the New Democratic party has himself on one occasion during the question period given an indication that a well known actuarial firm in its monthly newsletter referred in glowing tones to the government's actuarial report, and it is a fact that not one solitary voice in this country has demonstrated in any way or even attempted to attack the actuarial basis of the pension plan as being incorrect or fraudulent. The only attack upon this document has been made with respect to certain assumptions which have been made.
I am not an actuary, Mr. Speaker. My knowledge of pensions was practically nonexistent before I took this post, but I have done what I thought necessary and have worked to try to learn everything I could about pensions. However, I should like to make it perfectly clear that I have the utmost faith in those who prepared the actuarial report, and who prepared it without instructions as to what assumptions they would make.
I do not often use this word with approval, but the only instructions given the actuaries were that they were to use conservative estimates, and this they did. They prepared conservative estimates high and low. They showed to all who would read it what the plan would cost and, Mr. Speaker, we did not project it ten years, 25 years or 40 years. We projected it for nearly 100 years so that people could see what the basis was and, bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, not one person has attacked the reason for that plan.
Some assumptions have been attacked, one in particular with respect to the amount of unemployment in the short term. I repeat that no instructions were given by any representative of the government to the actuaries. They were told to use a conservative figure, and they used a figure of 6 per cent. Mr. Speaker, look at the figure produced the other day with regard to unemployment in Canada last month. I suggest to you that 6 per cent is, under a Liberal government, a

most conservative figure. Obviously therefore, if there are more people at work there will be produced, at the same rate of contribution, more money for the basis of the plan.
There were other assumptions which were attacked, some with respect to the longevity of our citizens and some with respect to the rate of immigration and the rate of fertility. These are actuarial assumptions and, in effect, as would be the case whether prepared by our actuaries or anyone else, these assumptions are educated guesses, because how can anyone in 1963 know with any degree of certainty what will be the situation of this country in 100 years? We do not know what the flow of immigration will be and what advances will be made with respect to the longevity of our people. But conservative estimates have been made, and high and low figures have been produced to indicate what the contribution rate will be.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in a personal attempt to find out everything I could about pension schemes, and as much as anything else to test my own belief in the public servants who were preparing this plan, I took three weeks during our break this summer and went to western Europe, to countries which are most closely comparable with Canada, to countries with which we must compete, to industrial countries, every one of which has in existence a national contributory pension scheme.
There is no question that the country to the south of us has had a similar type of scheme for some 30 odd years. The countries of Australia and New Zealand have also adopted such schemes, and they have realized, as has been suggested here, that flat rate pensions are not sufficient. I went to find out what the arguments against the introduction of such a scheme had been in countries like West Germany, Britain, France, Holland and the Scandinavian countries, and I found out that the spectres raised here were the same spectres raised by much the same interests in those countries prior to the adoption of their plans. I asked some things of government officials and ministers.
I should perhaps point out to hon. members that these plans have been enacted by almost the whole spectrum of governments in Europe, from rightist to leftist; but I asked why certain things were done, questions which cannot be answered by an exchange of correspondence but only by face to face confrontation. I at least satisfied myself that the people who worked out our plan knew exactly what they were doing. They had recourse to information respecting all these European plans, and we selected and put together what we thought was the 28902-5-266i

speechtext: May I ask the minister a question. Just as a matter of clarification, since she went to find out all the objections in European countries to this kind of scheme, could she explain to the house if she found out the real objections of Mr. Lesage and, if so, could she elaborate on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend raises this because I regret that I neglected to mention Quebec, in this particular context. Originally the question was asked of me why it was that I was directing fire against Ontario and not against Quebec. I should like to make this clear, because there is a simple answer. I am sure most hon. members of the house know the provisions of the British North America Act amendment which was enacted at the time the flat rate $40 a month old age security was brought into effect. Many people on the benches opposite and on these benches were here then. That rather peculiarly worded subsection says that there is concurrent jurisdiction in the provinces and in the federal government to deal with old age security, but that no federal legislation may affect present or future provincial legislation. Opinions have been taken as to what "affect" may mean- legal opinions from our department and the Department of Justice. It appears clear, however, that if the province occupies the field, covers it for all those in the province, makes it compulsory to all, and provides a sufficient plan, then there is no room for anyone else. There would be no room, in law, for the Canada pension plan, and not only might it be a danger to attempt to enforce it within our constitutional framework because of the social implications, but also because of the legal implications. For had the province of Quebec then attempted to fight off legally the Canada pension plan, it might have been decided to be ultra vires the federal parliament not only for Quebec but for all of Canada.
Accordingly when the resolution was enacted by the provincial legislation with Quebec declaring, as they have every right to do-and hon. members may look at the language-that they would enact a universal comprehensive plan, the federal government, in light of the legal situation and this one narrow piece of the B.N.A. Act, had absolutely no choice but to stand back from the borders of Quebec with respect to Canada pensions.

subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. lady a question. Does the government consider a resolution expressing an intention as occupying a field?

Pension Legislation Delayed

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I can only say this, that the resolution was passed unanimously by the provincial legislature, and that statements have been made by the premier which indicate that if the federal government acted precipitately to come into the field, a special session would be called and legislation introduced in Quebec. I suggest it really would not matter, because even if the Canada pension plan were first enacted and subsequently a provincial plan were enacted in the province of Quebec, the same effect would follow because of the phraseology of the B.N.A. Act. There is no question that I would prefer, and I think all hon. members would prefer, to have one plan to embrace our country. This is not possible under the present circumstances unless, as they may do, and as they have the right to do, and as I would entreat them to do, the representatives of Quebec within her provincial legislature reconsider the matter and come under the umbrella of one Canada-wide plan. This and this alone is the reason why no attack has been made on Quebec, why no entreaties have been held out to her, because her legal position is so very different from that of the province of Ontario.
I was speaking before about the attacks made against this scheme. I think at least a couple of hon. members have put a motion on the order paper asking for production of correspondence dealing with the Canada pension plan. We in my department have taken a box score of how these have been running. Letters from individuals have run three to one in favour of the Canada pension plan. However, I must confess that from organizations such as insurance companies and trust company offices almost the opposite ratio has been true. It now remains to educate those in the insurance and trust company field.

subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext: May I ask the hon. lady a question. If the government has given the plan such thorough study as the minister has indicated, why is it now proposed to refer the matter to a committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for his question, with which I was just about to deal. I should have thought from what I have said that it was clear that it was now necessary to educate insurance men and trust company men, and the only way we can educate them-

subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is the government which needs educating.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I realize we cannot get them elected to the backbenches in time to deal with this plan, but we must give them the opportunity to appear before the hon. members of this house, and I would hope of the
XMr. Douglas.]

other place, who would take under their hands the study of this legislation. There has been a request from many sources in the country for a study of the Canada pension plan by a committee of this place. This government has no intention despite this minister's personal desires for precipitate action, to stampede into action which is misunderstood and against which there has been a deliberate lobby of misinformation. Accordingly, there is only one way for the people of the country to understand what this plan is, and that is to lay it before the people's representatives for study. I would hope that that committee would be set up and would call before it those who have made public statements against the principle and the details of this legislation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, may I say to the house that I will, as I have in the past few weeks, make available all the information possible to any and every member of this house in order that they may discuss it with their constituents and with those who would oppose it. The government will take every opportunity to discuss the matter with provincial governments, for we hope that this will lead to close co-operation and the early introduction of the legislation and, in conjunction with the studies conducted by the provinces, provide the house the opportunity for further thorough study.
I still hope this plan can be brought in and passed by all members of this house in order that the timetable which has been referred to will be met. If I may mention the timetable, it may be recalled that the registration was to be in March 1964. We hope that registration will be proceeded with, for its purpose was not only for the Canada pension plan but for a couple of other governmental purposes, namely that of the unemployment insurance commission. It is our intention to proceed with the numbering or renumbering in early 1964, provided we are able to obtain the understanding of the provinces, and to have a thorough discussion of the question in committee. There seems no reason to suppose that we will not be able with care to make the original timetable. In short, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to my hon. friend that I am indeed grateful for this opportunity to clarify a few matters in the House of Commons, and to say that it is the intention of the government and of my ministry to continue with this legislation, which we believe will be for the betterment of all of our Canadian people.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, I would be happy to. It is the intention of the government, as soon as we reach orders of the day tomorrow, to go on with the second reading of the Income Tax Act, and then with the committee stage as soon as the second reading has been adopted. That will be the business also on Thursday. I have spoken to the hon. gentlemen opposite to whom I usually speak about these matters, and I understand there would be no objection, if the income tax measure should not be completed before five o'clock on Thursday, to going on with it on Thursday evening until such time as it is completed. If it should be completed before the end of the evening on Thursday I would arrange to have one of the ministers ready to go on with estimates for the rest of the evening until 10.30. Of course, on Friday evening we will take estimates. What I have in mind would be the Department of Forestry, with the estimates of the Department of Public Works available when the estimates of the Department of Forestry have been completed.
Business of the House
When the leader of the house suggests we continue on Thursday evening until the income tax measure is completed, he is suggesting, I take it, we go on until the usual hour of adjournment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Knowing how anxious hon. gentlemen opposite are to get on with the business of the country, I naturally assumed we would complete it.
Perhaps I should indicate what business would probably be taken up after the completion of the income tax measure. There is, I think, an understanding in all parts of the house that the motion in the name of the Solicitor General to refer the consumer credit question to a committee could be disposed of after one speaker from each part of the house has spoken for not more than 10 minutes. On that understanding, once the income tax measure has been completed, the government would be prepared to make this the next item of business. We would like to get the committee on the C.N.R. set up if it seemed feasible to get it through fairly quickly. We would like to oblige the hon. member for Brandon-Souris by getting second reading promptly of the two bills respecting the territories so that the committee can go on with them without delay; and there are one or two other matters which the government is prepared to move forward if there is an opportunity, so that we may get on with the Canada pension plan more quickly.
What estimates will be taken on Thursday night?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to consult my colleagues, to see who would be free, and I should also like to consult with hon. gentlemen in other parts of the house.
Are there to be estimates on Thursday night?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Only if we get through with the other business.
